reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a persistent, encapsulated collection of pancreatic fluid that develops weeks after acute or chronic pancreatitis, or after pancreatic trauma
Unlike a true cyst it lacks an epithelial lining and is bounded by a wall of fibrous and granulation tissue, requiring around four weeks to mature
Common presentations include persistent or recurrent upper abdominal pain, a palpable epigastric mass, early satiety, nausea, and failure to recover after an episode of pancreatitis
A raised serum amylase and high amylase within aspirated fluid support the diagnosis and help distinguish it from a cystic neoplasm
Contrast CT and endoscopic ultrasound define the collection, its relation to the stomach and duodenum, and any ductal communication
Many small, asymptomatic pseudocysts resolve spontaneously and can be observed, whereas large, symptomatic, enlarging, or complicated collections need drainage
Drainage is increasingly endoscopic (transmural cystgastrostomy or cystduodenostomy), with surgical internal drainage or percutaneous approaches reserved for selected cases
In older patients or those without a clear pancreatitis history, a cystic pancreatic neoplasm must be excluded before assuming a pseudocyst
reference.pathophysiology: Pancreatic pseudocysts arise when pancreatic ductal disruption, from acute inflammation, chronic pancreatitis, or trauma, allows enzyme-rich secretions to leak and collect in or around the pancreas. The surrounding tissue reacts, and over several weeks an inflammatory capsule of fibrous and granulation tissue forms, producing a mature pseudocyst without a true epithelial lining. Persistent communication with the pancreatic duct maintains the collection. Enlargement can compress adjacent structures, and complications develop when the cyst becomes infected, erodes into a vessel to form a pseudoaneurysm or bleed, or ruptures into the peritoneum or an adjacent viscus.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic pancreatic neoplasm (serous or mucinous cystadenoma, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm)
Acute peripancreatic fluid collection or walled-off necrosis
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to characterise the collection and its wall
Endoscopic ultrasound with fluid aspiration for amylase, CEA, and cytology to exclude a neoplasm
Serum amylase and lipase and liver function tests
MRCP or ERP to assess pancreatic ductal anatomy and communication before drainage
Ultrasound for follow-up of size in conservatively managed cysts
redFlags: Sudden severe pain, expanding mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding suggesting pseudoaneurysm erosion or rupture
Fever, rigors, and systemic sepsis indicating an infected pseudocyst
Progressive gastric outlet or biliary obstruction from a large cyst
Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting free rupture into the peritoneal cavity
reference.prognosis: Small uncomplicated pseudocysts frequently resolve without intervention, and drainage of symptomatic collections has good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with complications such as haemorrhage from a pseudoaneurysm, infection, or rupture, and recurrence is more likely when underlying ductal disease or chronic pancreatitis is not addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking a cystic pancreatic neoplasm for a pseudocyst and draining rather than resecting it
Draining a collection before the wall has matured, increasing the risk of leakage and failure
Overlooking an associated pseudoaneurysm, so that drainage precipitates torrential bleeding
Ignoring underlying pancreatic ductal obstruction, leading to recurrence after drainage
Delaying treatment of an infected pseudocyst presenting with sepsis
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Observation with serial imaging for small, asymptomatic pseudocysts, many of which resolve spontaneously
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided transmural drainage by cystgastrostomy or cystduodenostomy as first-line treatment for mature, symptomatic or enlarging collections
Endoscopic transpapillary drainage or pancreatic duct stenting where there is ductal communication
Surgical or percutaneous drainage when endoscopic drainage fails or the anatomy is unfavourable
Management of complications with antibiotics and drainage for infection and angiographic embolisation for pseudoaneurysm or haemorrhage
Supportive care with analgesia and nutrition and treatment of the underlying pancreatitis
Interval imaging follow-up to confirm resolution and detect recurrence
